slides.text:
One DSD People, Access and Culture
Equity in Budgets, Rates, Contracts, and Procurement
Examine what an allocation makes possible, where its burden lands, and what evidence supports a better option.
Advanced self-directed learning
slides.narration: A budget is also an account of what an organization makes possible. Money, staff time, materials, and selection requirements can shape who reaches a service and whose work receives support. This course examines those connections through fictional DSD examples. You will distinguish an amount from its distribution, consider necessary safeguards alongside participation, and prepare an explanation that respects actual fiscal and purchasing responsibilities. The goal is a substantive equity contribution to the decision, with clear assumptions and honest limits.

slides.text:
The total does not tell the whole story
Two proposals have the same total budget. One includes usable instructions and staff preparation; the other leaves people to find their own help.

Ask who carries the work outside the total. A smaller agency expense may shift time, difficulty, or cost to someone else.
slides.narration: Think about a service explanation that becomes shorter to prepare because staff no longer provide clarification. The recorded expense may decrease, while people spend more time finding answers or staff handle repeated confusion later. These effects need examination rather than assumption. A resource analysis follows what the proposal pays for and what it expects others to supply. Repeating an unsupported expectation across services can make a barrier ordinary, even when each separate budget appears reasonable when read only as a total.

slides.text:
Distribution means opportunity and burden
Identify the resource, its intended purpose, the people who can use it, and the work someone else must carry.

Equal amounts, support fitted to need, and protection of essential access answer different questions. Explain which meaning of fairness the proposal uses.
slides.narration: An equal amount can be a meaningful starting point, but it does not establish that circumstances are alike. A team may need different preparation to complete the same task, or an application may impose different burdens depending on available support. Advanced analysis makes the chosen principle visible. Ask why it fits the purpose and what evidence would challenge it. The inquiry is about actual conditions and opportunity; it does not presume that every difference in resources is unfair or that equal amounts are always sufficient.

slides.text:
Worked example: capacity or the service?
A fictional purchasing proposal requires a large administrative office. Its purpose is reliable delivery and reporting.

Compare office size with evidence of delivery, usable records, and reporting capacity. A different route could preserve safeguards without assuming size proves quality.
slides.narration: The proposed requirement names an organizational feature, while the purpose concerns reliable work. A large office may support that work, but its size alone does not demonstrate delivery or exclude every smaller provider from competence. Compare the requirement with evidence of the actual capacity needed. A focused alternative might examine reporting arrangements and relevant experience. It remains a proposal to evaluate through the applicable process. Removing a necessary safeguard would be a poor response; examining whether the stated feature serves that safeguard is a useful equity question.

slides.text:
A requirement larger than its purpose
A fictional contract proposal requires a large administrative office to ensure reliable reporting. A smaller organization describes a workable reporting arrangement. What is the strongest equity response?
A. Examine the actual reporting capacity and compare a focused alternative through the applicable process.
B. Keep office size because an established organization is always safer.
C. Remove every reporting safeguard so all organizations can participate.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.
slides.narration: In this fictional proposal, reliable reporting is the purpose and office size is the proposed way to demonstrate it. A smaller organization offers an account of its reporting arrangement. You are examining the requirement, not selecting a contractor. Consider which response preserves the substantive safeguard while allowing relevant evidence to be considered. The systemic question is what happens when size repeatedly stands in for capacity across opportunities. Neither the concern nor the alternative establishes eligibility, an award, or service results. Choose the strongest analysis response.

links.name: Answer 1
links.text: A. Examine the actual reporting capacity and compare a focused alternative through the applicable process.

links.name: Answer 2
links.text: B. Keep office size because an established organization is always safer.

links.name: Answer 3
links.text: C. Remove every reporting safeguard so all organizations can participate.

slides.text:
Why this response helps
Examine the capacity needed, not size alone. Repeated size gates may narrow service reach; compare relevant reporting evidence and a feasible alternative. No award, eligibility, or improved access is established.

Which feature in a requirement demonstrates the capacity actually needed?
Continue learning
Try another response
slides.narration: This response connects the purpose with evidence of the actual work. A focused alternative could preserve reporting safeguards while allowing more than one organizational arrangement to demonstrate capacity. Repeated reliance on size alone may narrow who can participate and whose services become available. Examine requirements and feasibility through the actual process; the fictional account does not establish an award or improved access.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
Size may support capacity, but it does not prove reliability. Repeating that substitute can exclude relevant evidence. Examine actual reporting arrangements and necessary safeguards; the outcome remains unknown.

Which feature in a requirement demonstrates the capacity actually needed?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: An established office can support reporting, but the scenario does not show that it always does or that a smaller arrangement cannot. Treating the feature as conclusive bypasses the relevant evidence and may repeatedly narrow participation. A better response asks what reliable reporting requires and how each applicant demonstrates it. The available information does not settle eligibility or comparative capacity.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
Removing safeguards could undermine the public purpose. Compare ways to demonstrate reporting capacity while addressing the size gate. Wider participation or better services still require evidence.

Which feature in a requirement demonstrates the capacity actually needed?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: Reporting safeguards may protect the public purpose and cannot simply be discarded in the name of participation. The equity inquiry examines whether the particular size requirement is necessary to meet them. Compare feasible evidence routes and their burdens. A broader invitation can be meaningful without establishing an award, provider quality, or the distribution of later service results.

slides.text:
Follow the burden to its carrier
An instruction may assume spare administrative time, reliable technology, transport, or unpaid help.

Trace whose effort makes the proposal workable. A hidden burden can affect service participation and the staff who repeatedly help people navigate it.
slides.narration: Imagine that an application requires information already provided in a different form. An organization with administrative support may assemble it easily; another may divert service time to do the same work. This does not tell us whether the requirement is unnecessary, but it identifies a burden worth examining. Ask what information is needed and whether an existing usable account can meet the purpose. If the same avoidable task recurs at every stage, the accumulated burden may shape participation much more than the invitation suggests.

slides.text:
Trace who carries the work
Proposed relationship for practice
1. Proposed requirement
2. Resources paid for
3. Work left outside
4. Who carries that work?
5. Participation to examine
Which assumption about unpaid work needs evidence before comparing options?
A budget total may leave some work outside the agency expense. Examine whether that effort changes practical participation.
slides.narration:
CONCEPTUAL INQUIRY MAP: connections identify questions, not a measured causal sequence.

A budget total may leave some work outside the agency expense. Examine whether that effort changes practical participation.

Which assumption about unpaid work needs evidence before comparing options?

The map does not prove a transferred cost, mandate new payment, or establish participation effects. Actual mechanisms, permissions, and responsibilities still apply.

slides.text:
Keep funding mechanisms distinct
A grant supports an authorized public purpose. Procurement acquires goods or services; other payments have their own arrangements.

Establish which mechanism you are examining and the applicable requirements. An equity proposal does not supply approval, award authority, or permission to change an agreement.
slides.narration: The Minnesota Office of Grants Management distinguishes grants from procurement and other payments. That distinction matters because a useful participation idea must fit the actual arrangement. The consultant can examine a barrier and offer a substantive alternative alongside fiscal, program, or legislative expertise. The analysis does not replace the responsibilities held by those who manage the mechanism. Begin with the actual purpose and requirements rather than borrowing a grant procedure for a purchase or assuming a supportive recommendation can change an existing agreement.

slides.text:
A usable invitation is part of participation
A fictional opportunity is explained only in an image-based document. An applicant cannot read its requirements with their usual reading tool.

Examine the document and offer a usable explanation through the actual process. Do not infer competence, eligibility, or organizational size from the access difficulty.
slides.narration: The observed problem concerns receiving the explanation, not the applicant’s ability to perform the funded work. If the invitation repeatedly excludes people who cannot use that format, later reviewers may see fewer applications and mistake the absence for lack of interest. A usable explanation can address this entry barrier while preserving substantive requirements. Examine whether applicants receive equivalent information and how questions are answered. Correcting the route does not establish that someone is eligible or that the later selection will have equitable results.

slides.text:
Criteria need a reason connected to the work
Identify what each criterion measures and why that matters for the purpose.

Distinguish demonstrated capacity from familiar presentation, existing networks, or polished language. Apply the same relevant questions while examining whether every applicant could understand the invitation.
slides.narration: A proposal can be clearly written and still leave an important service question unanswered. Another may use unfamiliar language while providing strong evidence of the work required. Criteria help reviewers focus on that substance when they are defined and applied consistently. Examine whether a familiar presentation style has become an unspoken substitute for capacity. Repeated use of such a substitute can narrow opportunity. The answer is a better account of the criterion and its evidence, not automatic preference for any applicant or removal of legitimate standards.

slides.text:
Worked comparison: the average hides a gap
FICTIONAL: four providers each deliver 10 units. Their assumed costs are $80, $120, $100, and $180: $480 total.

Paying $12 per unit gives each $120, also $480 total. The fourth still has a $60 gap. A matched total does not establish adequacy for each provider.
slides.narration: Read the assumptions carefully. Each fictional provider delivers ten identical units; the exercise assigns different total costs. A twelve-dollar payment per unit gives each provider one hundred twenty dollars. The combined payment matches the combined assumed cost, yet the distribution does not match every provider’s cost. This comparison demonstrates arithmetic under invented conditions, not actual DHS rates or service results. Before proposing a response, examine why costs differ, whether the unit comparison is appropriate, and what resources and requirements a real decision must consider.

slides.text:

What explains different costs, and what evidence would support a real rate recommendation?

slides.text:
When a budget saves by shifting the work
A fictional budget removes usable onboarding materials but retains visible development projects. New staff must find their own explanations before joining those projects. What should the analysis examine?
A. Only the agency expense saved; preparation outside the budget is personal responsibility.
B. Preparation burden and access to projects across the employee life cycle, with feasible alternatives.
C. A smaller budget proves that particular employees will not advance.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.
slides.narration: A saving in one budget line can leave work to be completed somewhere else. In this fictional team, the removed materials helped new staff understand how to join development projects. Those projects may later provide experience and evidence relevant to advancement. Consider which response follows that connection without assuming a particular employee result. The analysis can compare feasible ways to preserve necessary preparation and identify evidence about access. It should not treat unpaid effort as automatically available or infer discrimination from the proposal alone. Choose the most useful inquiry.

links.name: Answer 1
links.text: A. Only the agency expense saved; preparation outside the budget is personal responsibility.

links.name: Answer 2
links.text: B. Preparation burden and access to projects across the employee life cycle, with feasible alternatives.

links.name: Answer 3
links.text: C. A smaller budget proves that particular employees will not advance.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
Counting only the expense hides preparation shifted to staff. Repeating that gap may shape later project access. Examine usable onboarding and alternatives; the size or distribution of the effect is unknown.

Which later opportunity depends on the preparation a proposal leaves unfunded?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: The recorded expense matters, but it does not describe all work needed for the arrangement to function. Leaving preparation to employees can repeatedly affect entry to development projects, especially when established staff already have usable explanations. Examine actual burden and feasible support rather than treating it as irrelevant. The scenario does not establish how many people are affected or their later outcomes.

slides.text:
Why this response helps
Trace the shifted preparation, project entry, and later opportunity. Compare feasible ways to preserve necessary support. Repeated unsupported entry may sustain unequal conditions, but advancement effects are not established.

Which later opportunity depends on the preparation a proposal leaves unfunded?
Continue learning
Try another response
slides.narration: This response follows the resource decision through onboarding, project access, and later employee opportunity. It identifies a plausible recurring mechanism while retaining uncertainty about effects. Compare necessary preparation with feasible alternatives and examine who can use them. A supported concern can justify inquiry without becoming a performance judgment, an assumption about identity, or a claim that a particular advancement result has occurred.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
The budget identifies a possible pathway, not a proven employee outcome. Examine support, project entry, and later evidence. A focused alternative can address the gate without assuming the cause or result.

Which later opportunity depends on the preparation a proposal leaves unfunded?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: The proposal may create a meaningful access concern, but it cannot establish an individual employee’s future advancement. Other conditions and decisions also matter. A better account explains the preparation gap and how it could recur, then compares support options and relevant evidence. Keep the possible mechanism visible while avoiding a prediction presented as a proven outcome.

slides.text:
Workforce resources shape later opportunity
Removing onboarding support and accessible materials may leave new staff doing extra preparation while established staff retain visible assignments.

Trace the connection from recruitment and onboarding to development, performance evidence, advancement, and retention. The proposal’s wording does not establish the later effects.
slides.narration: A resource decision can influence more than the activity removed. If an employee must solve an avoidable access difficulty alone, less time may remain for the assignment that later demonstrates readiness. Staff with established support may not face that same condition. Examine the proposed change through the employee life cycle, including supervision and development. A plausible pathway identifies what to investigate; it does not establish a particular employee’s performance or a population disparity. Better comparison asks which essential conditions each option preserves and who supplies the remaining work.

slides.text:
Compare feasible options and their tradeoffs
Compare the baseline, the proposed change, and a focused alternative using the same purpose and evidence.

Consider service reach, necessary safeguards, practical capacity, who carries costs, and uncertainty. A compelling equity concern still needs a workable response.
slides.narration: An alternative might retain usable onboarding support while changing a less essential activity, or replace an office-size requirement with evidence of actual delivery capacity. Each response has tradeoffs. Compare them openly rather than presenting the preferred option as costless. The legislative analyst, program staff, and consultant can contribute different parts of the explanation while preserving existing responsibilities. If an alternative cannot yet be costed or its arrangement is unclear, describe that gap. Unknown feasibility deserves further examination, not a favorable score or an invented zero.

slides.text:
A fiscal estimate has a defined scope
State budget estimates and wider effects answer related but different questions.

Identify the period, units, assumptions, and costs included. Keep uncounted participant or workforce burden visible as a separate inquiry; do not add it to an official estimate without a fitting basis.
slides.narration: The Minnesota budget resources explain the role of fiscal notes in estimating effects on the state budget. An equity explanation can also examine conditions that the estimate does not establish, such as whether a person can use the service route or whose unpaid work makes it possible. Keep those inquiries distinct. A wider effect is not automatically an additional state expenditure, and an official cost estimate is not proof of a service result. Clear scope helps colleagues use each account without mistaking one for the other.

slides.text:
Community knowledge can reveal hidden work
Ask people affected by the proposed allocation what effort the current arrangement requires and what the alternative would change.

Culture briefs can help prepare respectful questions. Actual accounts, not a group description, inform the burden analysis. No partner speaks for every person.
slides.narration: A proposal may assume that family help, digital access, or flexible time is readily available. Community engagement can show where that assumption needs examination and what the task means in a person’s life. A culture brief may help you notice a question about communication or support, but it cannot establish someone’s resources or preferences. Invite relevant perspectives without demanding personal disclosure. Read the accounts alongside the proposal, practical evidence, and missing perspectives, and explain whose experience is present before drawing conclusions about the wider population.

slides.text:
Participation needs a place in the decision
Explain what is open to change, what is already constrained, and how relevant input will be considered.

Receiving comments does not establish influence. Record the substantive concern faithfully and explain how it affects the comparison—or why it cannot yet answer the question.
slides.narration: When people describe a burden, the useful next step is to connect that account to the option being examined. An invitation becomes misleading if it implies that every condition is open when some are fixed. Be clear about the actual space for influence and retain the meaning of contributions. Repeating a consultation that produces no visible account of the concern can erode trust. A responsible explanation describes the issue, the response within actual responsibilities, and the evidence still needed, without promising an award or a resource change.

slides.text:
A community account of the hidden burden
People describe unpaid help needed to complete a fictional funding application. A culture brief raised useful preparation questions. Which conclusion best fits the evidence?
A. The brief proves every member of that community needs unpaid assistance.
B. Receiving comments establishes that the revised application will be accessible.
C. The accounts identify a burden to examine; compare usable routes and explain whose experience is present.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.
slides.narration: The culture brief helped staff prepare questions, and people now describe the work needed to complete the fictional application. Their accounts can reveal a burden omitted from the budget. They do not establish the experience of every person or the success of a proposed revision. Consider which conclusion preserves the meaning of these contributions and connects it with a practical comparison. The question is whether repeated assumptions about unpaid help narrow participation, and what usable alternatives might address that gate within the actual requirements. Choose the strongest conclusion.

links.name: Answer 1
links.text: A. The brief proves every member of that community needs unpaid assistance.

links.name: Answer 2
links.text: B. Receiving comments establishes that the revised application will be accessible.

links.name: Answer 3
links.text: C. The accounts identify a burden to examine; compare usable routes and explain whose experience is present.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
A brief prepares questions; it is not evidence about every person. Repeating a group assumption can misdirect resources. Examine actual accounts and usable alternatives, with missing perspectives kept visible.

Whose work does a proposed application assume will be available?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: Turning preparation material into a population finding replaces people’s own accounts with a group assumption. That may repeatedly direct resources toward an inaccurate explanation of need. Use the brief to improve questions, then examine what participants actually describe and what the arrangement requires. Missing perspectives remain important; the scenario does not establish that every person relies on the same assistance.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
Comments provide relevant experience, not proof that the arrangement works. Repeated invitations without a substantive response can sustain the barrier. Compare routes and explain the response; later access is unknown.

Whose work does a proposed application assume will be available?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: Receiving comments is evidence of participation in the inquiry, not proof of a usable application or later access. If the burden is repeatedly heard without affecting the comparison, the same gate may remain. Explain what the accounts show and how a feasible response would address it. Keep approval, actual use, and the distribution of results as separate questions.

slides.text:
Why this response helps
Use the accounts to examine shifted work and alternatives. Repeated unpaid-help assumptions may narrow participation. Preserve individual meaning and missing perspectives; neither the brief nor these accounts proves a population result.

Whose work does a proposed application assume will be available?
Continue learning
Try another response
slides.narration: This conclusion connects lived experience with the practical requirement while preserving its scope. An assumed supply of unpaid help can repeatedly shape who completes an application. Compare feasible routes that meet necessary requirements and explain how the burden informs the analysis. Preserve individual meaning, missing perspectives, and unknown results rather than treating the brief or the comments as a population guarantee.

slides.text:
Make the equity explanation useful
Name the proposal and purpose, the allocation or requirement, the evidence of a possible barrier, and the alternatives.

State the distribution and assumptions, relevant ADSA goal when useful, limits, and the recommendation’s basis. Preserve fiscal and purchasing responsibilities.
slides.narration: A concise equity explanation should help colleagues understand the decision rather than add a separate layer of vague language. Show which requirement or resource pattern matters and how it may affect service access or workforce opportunity. Relevant ADSA goals can explain why the concern belongs in the division’s work; they do not supply evidence or approval. The consultant contributes substantive analysis with colleagues, while the legislative director, deputy, strategic development coordinator, division director, and Equity Director retain their existing responsibilities. Do not invent a new approval chain.

slides.text:
Examine use after an actual change
A revised amount or requirement is evidence of a change in the arrangement. Service reach, burden, quality, and participation require their own evidence.

Look for repeated conditions and unintended effects. A favorable total can coexist with an unresolved barrier.
slides.narration: If a requirement is revised, that is a real change worth describing accurately. It does not establish that organizations could participate or people received the intended support. Examine how the arrangement is used and whether the earlier concern persists in another form. A change that helps entry may introduce a later reporting burden; a larger payment may not resolve the service condition originally identified. Keeping these distinctions visible supports a justified decision about what to retain, revise, or investigate rather than a premature declaration of success.

slides.text:
Rewrite a claim that exceeds the evidence
Original: “The $480 payment covers everyone fairly.”

A supported revision: “The fictional total matches assumed total cost, but the $120 payment leaves one provider $60 below its assumed cost.”

What evidence would you need before recommending a real rate change?
slides.narration: Try rewriting the original sentence in your own words before reading the example. The revision keeps what the arithmetic establishes and makes its distribution visible. It does not declare a real payment inadequate, identify why costs differ, or claim that a particular rate would improve services. Those are further questions. This habit matters whenever a simple total becomes a broad conclusion. Keeping assumptions, differences, and purpose together allows colleagues to examine the concern and the alternative without being asked to accept an unsupported judgment.

slides.text:
Reflect on what fairness requires here
Choose a resource decision familiar to you. What purpose does it serve, which conditions make participation possible, and who supplies work outside the budget?

Keep the reflection private if you wish. Identify one necessary safeguard and one assumption worth examining.
slides.narration: Your own experience may reveal a resource pattern that is hard to see in a spreadsheet. Consider a time when support made participation possible, or when an apparently equal arrangement required very different effort. You do not need to disclose identity or a personal story. Use the reflection to sharpen a work question rather than diagnose anyone’s motives. Separating a necessary safeguard from an unexamined assumption can help you preserve meaningful standards while considering a more usable route to service or employee opportunity.

slides.text:
A recommendation with substance and limits
Read the total and the distribution. Examine purpose, participation, safeguards, and shifted burden.

Compare workable alternatives and preserve the evidence, assumptions, and actual responsibilities. A supported recommendation makes the next decision clearer without promising an unmeasured result.
slides.narration: The central question is what a resource decision makes possible and whose work supports it. Carry that question through the amount, the requirements, the comparison, and actual use. Equity analysis is strongest when it is precise about both the possible barrier and a practical response. You can contribute useful evidence and recommendations without replacing fiscal or procurement responsibilities. Keep fictional figures separate from real estimates, and leave unknown results open. That clarity helps the division connect resources with the service and workplace conditions it intends to support.

outcomes: Trace where resources, opportunity, and uncompensated burden are distributed.
Identify a participation barrier inside a proposed requirement.
Compare allocation or selection options using clear criteria and fitting evidence.
Prepare an equity explanation that preserves actual budget and procurement responsibilities.
